Raul: Ethan, can I ask you something?
Ethan: Sure, shoot.
Raul: I have to make this app communicate to the mail server to send daily newsfeed to the subscribers as the teacher asked us to, but I don't remember how to do it.
Ethan: Well, that can be the easiest thing depending on what framework you use. What are you going to use to do it?
Raul: Well, I think I'll use Oracle. It is the one I remember the most.

Ethan: Why aren't you going to use .NET? I think it is the wisest option as you are working with Windows.
Raul: Well, I haven't thought about it, but now that you mention it, that could be a really good idea.
Ethan: Say no more. Let's see, I think the most intelligent way to do it is by using delegates as it's an event-driven application.
Raul: Wait, what?
Ethan: Hmmm, I see. You didn't come to that class. Let's imagine that every time you click on a button, it automatically generates an event or action. That is a line of code one can handle, and an event-driven application is an app that executes or invokes code as a response to any event.
Raul: I see.

Ethan: Therefore, as in your case, where you need to concatenate loose objects, the best way to do so is by using delegates. They bind pointers that lead to specific code. The fact of clicking over a submit button after having filled a form, for example, generates an event, but that event needs a delegate that equates to a function pointer. Such pointer only references to a specific function, making it type-safe and secure. Consequently, a delegate consists of a function pointer heading to a specific object and references to one or many other methods within the object.

The Future With Going to in Questions
We use going to in the interrogative form to ask about future plans, actions or events.

First of all, let's have a quick review of the general structure. Remember that plans and arrangements are commonly expressed using this structure:

Subject + verb to be + going to + main verb + complement

Let's see an example of this:

My assistant is going to call the software manager tomorrow.

Now, that's the structure for affirmative statements; the negative structure is similar, with only one difference: we add the particle not after the verb to be. But right now, we will focus on the interrogative form, which allows us to ask about plans and arrangements for the future. The structure of the interrogative form that we use for this purpose is:

Verb to be + subject + going to + main verb + complement +?


Something important to notice is that this type of questions are close-ended; this means that the answer to them is usually yes/no/I don't know. Let's take a look at a couple of interactions where this structure is used:

Examples:
A: Are you going to reinstall the antivirus software?
B: Yes, I am, but not today; maybe tomorrow morning.

A: Is this software update going to support our old drivers?
B: I don't know, we should ask the IT manager.

As you know, there are also questions that need a full sentence as an answer; these are called wh-questions. This is the grammatical structure used in this case:

Interrogative adverb (what, where, when, etc.) + verb to be + subject + going to + main verb + complement +?


Examples:
A: What are you going to use for designing the website?
B: I'm going to use an event-driven programming.
What are you going to use to do it?
Why aren't you going to use .NET?
Superlatives
We use the superlative form of adjectives to express the extreme point of a quality, feature or characteristic.

At this point, you are already familiar with adjectives; they are words that express features, qualities and characteristics of nouns:

The computers in this office are very old.
There is a big update coming next year.

And, of course, sometimes we want to compare two or more people or things based on one of their common characteristics, features or qualities. For that purpose, we use comparative and superlative forms of adjectives. Today, we will focus on superlatives; let's take a look at the chart below to learn the superlatives of some common adjectives:

Superlatives are useful when we want to express that a noun has the extreme point of a quality, compared to other nouns.

As you may have noticed, some superlatives are formed with the suffix –est, and others with the words the most before the adjective. There is a rule that you can learn to form the superlative of the vast majority of adjectives:

Adjectives with one and two syllables= The (adjective)–est
Adjectives with three or more syllables= The most (adjective)

Examples:
    Jennifer is the most intelligent programmer I know.
    This cloud service software is the safest in the industry right now.
